title: What is hypothesis-driven thinking, and why do consultants guess early?
description: What a hypothesis is in a case interview, why stating one early makes you faster and clearer, and how to change your mind gracefully.
hook: It can feel wrong to guess the answer before you have seen any data. At school we were taught to collect evidence first and conclude later. Consulting works the other way round: you make an early, educated guess, then test it. This is not arrogance; it is efficiency. With a clear guess, you know which data to ask for, and you stop wandering.
body:
What a hypothesis is

A hypothesis is your current best guess at the answer, stated so it can be proved or disproved. "I suspect the profit fall is driven by rising delivery costs" is a hypothesis. "Let's look at costs" is not; it does not commit to anything you can test.

Why it helps

  • It focuses you. Instead of analysing everything, you look first where the answer most likely is.
  • It shows judgement. Interviewers want to see that you can form a view from limited information, as you would with a real client.
  • It makes the case a conversation. The interviewer can confirm or redirect you early.

Where good hypotheses come from

From the prompt itself (what is unusual?), from how the business makes money, and from common patterns. If sales are flat but profit fell, the problem is probably costs or mix, not volume. If one region is mentioned in the prompt, it is often mentioned for a reason.

Changing your mind is part of it

A hypothesis is meant to be tested, and sometimes the data says no. That is a good moment, not a bad one. Say it clearly: "That rules out costs. The numbers point to pricing instead, so I'd like to look there next." Candidates who hold on to a wrong guess lose marks; candidates who update calmly gain them.

Phrases to use

My initial hypothesis is that... so I'd like to start by checking...
That doesn't support my hypothesis. Given this, I now think... and I'd like to test that next.

Design a test that could prove your idea wrong

A hotel reports falling revenue. You suspect lower occupancy caused the decline. That is a testable hypothesis because the data can contradict it: if occupancy stayed constant and average daily rate fell, your initial explanation is wrong.

Suppose occupancy drops from 80% to 70% at 100 rooms, while the average room rate stays at £120. Daily room revenue falls from £9,600 to £8,400, a £1,200 loss. Your hypothesis has numerical support. But investigate whether occupancy fell because of competition, a renovation, seasonality or channel mix before recommending discounts.

A useful working hypothesis includes a prediction: "If competitor entry caused our decline, the affected hotels should be closest to the new rival and the timing should match its opening." Ask for data that might falsify that prediction, not just data that makes your idea sound plausible. Update your hypothesis when the evidence changes. Interviewers reward the quality of the reasoning, not attachment to your first guess.
